newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Hong Kong treaties apply to China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Hong Kong treaties apply to China.

text.p: An assistant U.S. attorney told a U.S. Appeals Court on Wednesday that the United States does not need Senate approval to extend treaties covering Hong Kong after the British colony reverts to Chinese control.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Alex Whiting asked the court to overturn a U.S. District Court's decision not to extradite a former tobacco executive wanted in Hong Kong on bribery charges because he would effectively be tried in Chinese courts.

In January, the chief judge of the U.S. District Court in Boston ruled that the U.S. extradition treaty with Britain covering Hong Kong was not intended to apply to a nondemocratic regime such as China.

Lawyers for former tobacco executive Lui Kin-Hong, also known as Jerry Lui, had argued that he would probably be tried after Hong Kong reverts back to China on July 1, and could face a quick trial and possibly be executed.
Judge Joseph Tauro's decision raised howls of protest from Hong Kong officials and threw into doubt the U.S. extradition treaty with the British colony.

China has promised to maintain British common law in Hong Kong after it reverts from 150 years of British rule. But Hong Kong Gov. Chris Patten has blasted China recently for proposing to dilute civil liberties laws in the territory.
"All treaties remain in force up to the reversion, and, if possible, after the reversion," Whiting said on Wednesday.
He told Judge Michael Boudin that he was correct to assume the Clinton administration could extend current treaties with Hong Kong without approval from two-thirds of the Senate.
But Whiting asked the court to disregard the larger political question and focus only on the current extradition treaty.
"Today, we are proceeding under a current, valid treaty," he said. "The analysis begins and ends with the treaty itself."
Besides, the Senate agreed in passing the 1992 United States-Hong Kong Policy Act to allow current treaties to remain in effect after reversion, he said.
Lui's lawyer, Andrew Good, said the government's policy toward China has undergone a "profound change" without approval from the U.S. Senate as required by the Constitution.
"What's happening here is terribly frightening," he told the court.
The treaty specifically states that those extradited to Hong Kong must be tried by British courts, he said.
"This is a U.K. specific treaty," he said. "The political question has to be answered by two-thirds of the Senate," he added.
If extradited to Hong Kong, Lui would be "sent to some gulag somewhere," he said.

Lui has been held in a Plymouth, Massachusetts, prison since he was captured at Boston's Logan Airport in December 1995 while in the United States to visit a sick friend. He has has been charged in Hong Kong of accepting bribes of $4.5 million in cash and loans.
A former export director with British-American Tobacco (Hong Kong) Ltd., Lui maintains his innoncence and said he has been framed by Hong Kong authorities.
